The emphasis on neat hair styling suggests a consumer focus on polished, tidy looks and sleek styles. The growing interest in non-toxic hair products reflects the broader consumer shift towards cleaner, safer ingredients. Weightless and lightweight benefits signify a demand for haircare solutions that offer volume and style without weighing hair down, catering to those seeking natural and airy styles. The trend of frizz control highlights a universal consumer need for managing and taming hair, indicating a preference for sleek and controlled hairstyles in varying environments. These benefits collectively represent a consumer-driven pursuit for polished, healthy and manageable hair styling solutions.

Popular searches indicate a strong interest in cognitive health and mental clarity (as evidenced by lion’s mane and saffron supplements); a focus on anti-aging and longevity (seen in NMN and magnesium bisglycinate searches), and a growing concern for digestive health and detoxification (highlighted by the popularity of parasite cleanse products). These trends signify consumers’ desire to take a proactive approach to their health, emphasising both physical and mental wellness.

These brands embody themes such as a return to traditional and ancient remedies, as seen in Ancient Nutrition and the holistic approach to wellness in Cymbiotika. JSHealth and Arrae indicate a focus on personalised health, while Bioray reflects growing interest in detoxification and overall wellbeing. These trends demonstrate consumers’ desire for effective and natural alternatives to support their health and vitality.

NMN and tocotrienols underscore a strong emphasis on anti-aging and longevity, reflecting a desire for long-term health. Lion’s mane suggests a growing interest in cognitive wellbeing and mental health. Fulvic acid highlights a trend towards natural and holistic health solutions, while cayenne pepper signifies a broader interest in incorporating functional foods into one's diet, indicating a desire for wellness through dietary choices. These trends collectively demonstrate consumers’ proactive approach to health and a focus on holistic wellbeing.

Top-growing bodycare trends reflect how consumers are seeking more innovative and diverse skincare solutions. A rise in searches for glycolic body lotion and hyaluronic acid body lotion point to a growing interest in ingredient-driven body care, as well as an emphasis on chemical exfoliation and deep hydration for the body. The surge in searches for anti-chafe products and body cloths reflects a desire for comfort and practicality in daily skincare routines, as well as preventing skin irritation and maintaining cleanliness.

Growth in searches for Naturium and Drunk Elephant suggests a focus on clean, science-driven body care, with consumers prioritising products that are effective and free from harmful ingredients. Patrick Ta's rise reflects a trend towards body makeup infused with good-for-you ingredients, while Eos' presence points to a demand for convenient and sustainable packaging in body care products. Maison Francis Kurkdjian signifies a preference for luxury and fragrance-infused body care, showcasing consumers' interest in elevating their daily skincare routines. It's interesting to note that many of the top brands are also makeup or skincare-native but have recently segued into body care.

Sustained growth in searches for hyaluronic acid suggests an emphasis on deep hydration and moisture retention in bodycare products, reflecting a desire for smooth and supple skin. The popularity of sesame oil and rose oil demonstrates a preference for natural and organic ingredients, aligning with a growing interest in holistic and botanical skincare solutions. Magnesium's presence highlights a focus on soothing and muscle-relief benefits in body care, possibly driven by consumers seeking relaxation and stress relief. The inclusion of benzoyl peroxide points to a need for acne-fighting solutions in bodycare.

Top-growing fragrance trends reveal consumers’ quest for unique or exotic experiences through scent, whether through spiritual and holistic scents like agarwood incense, unconventional and food-inspired aromas like pistachio and tomato, or the allure of rich, opulent Arabian scents. The interest in pheromone perfumes reflects consumers’ curiosity about the potential emotional and physiological impacts of fragrances. Across these trends, consumers are seeking personal and distinctive olfactory journeys that go beyond conventional fragrance choices.

Consumers are increasingly drawn to unique and niche brands like Tamburin and Dedcool, indicating a desire for individuality and distinctive scents beyond mainstream options. The popularity of Dime Beauty suggests a growing emphasis on clean and sustainable beauty. Ex Nihilo's rising profile suggests a willingness among consumers to invest in luxury fragrances, while By Rosie Jane may signify an interest in fragrance lines with a personal touch or unique storytelling, aligning with a desire for more meaningful scent experiences.

Growing interest in pistachio scents highlights a desire for unique and unconventional notes, while vanilla represents a timeless preference for comforting and familiar fragrances. The appearance of tomato hints at a growing interest in fresh and botanical notes, aligning with the trend for natural and organic ingredients. Amber oil and freesia signify a continued fascination with luxurious scent profiles, indicating a demand for richness and elegance in fragrances.

Top nail trends including silver chrome nails and lip gloss nails reveal an interest in shiny finishes this season. Searches for rubber base gel and semi-cured gel nails indicate that consumers are looking for new formats of nail products. The growing trend of comic book nails highlights an interest in a playful and dynamic nail look.

Press-on nails are seeing a resurgence as searches for Pear Nova and Glamnetic increase. Other top-trending brands including Nine Zero Lacquer, Rogue Lacquer and ILNP push bright and multi-dimensional polish colours. Overall, consumers continue to seek opportunities to play and create exciting looks at home, creating an opportunity for all nail brands.

An increase in searches for nail finishes such as metallic, shimmer and iridescent indicate consumer interest in multidimensional polishes. Frosted nail polish colours are also seeing a boost, indicating a nostalgic re-emergence of the look. Searches are also on the rise for red wine nail polish, revealing consumers are looking for warm moody tones this autumn — bonus points that the look is named after a classic food or beverage, a popular trend among younger consumers on social media.

Searches for moxi laser and nano needling reveal that consumers are seeking out in-office procedures even if they are pricier than at-home solutions. The growth in searches for modelling masks highlight consumers’ desire for a mask product with a visual impact.

Consumer driven searches for top skincare brands highlight the impact of branding; Pharmaciopy and Agency Skincare are driven by searches for the brand itself as opposed to searches for specific products.

Top growing ingredients are driven by specific products. Top searches for polypeptides are driven by Drunk Elephant’s Protini Polypeptide Cream. Searches for snail mucin are primarily for Cosrx's viral snail mucin essence. The top volume searches for seaweed come from an interest in Mario Badescu’s face mask and night cream. The other growing ingredients — polyglutamic acid and copper peptides — are driven by The Inkey List and The Ordinary, respectively.

Top-growing searches for hair pre-wash, hair-bonding treatments and chebe hair butter indicate consumers don’t mind adding extra steps if it will help hair health or growth. The increase in searches for dry shampoo powder and shampoo bars reveals consumer interest in specific product formats this summer.

Searches for hair brands such as Dae Hair, Doterra, and Acure are being driven by the brand names themselves, as well as indicating increased searches for classic shampoo and conditioner products. Whereas, searches for Coco and Eve and Not Your Mother's are product-specific, as consumers seek hair masks and dry shampoo.

Searches for chebe oil, and even some for jojoba oil, indicate consumers are looking toward natural ingredients to help stimulate hair growth. Searches for ciclopirox and baking soda in the context of hair reveal that the consumer is concerned with scalp health and dandruff.

The growth in searches for GLA and astaxanthin supplements indicates that the educated consumer is early in their knowledge of these supplements, and their potential ability to help repair skin from within. It could be a good opportunity for brands to create educational content around the product and make a play to own the space. Searches for leptin supplements reveal that consumers are continuously looking for new ways to lose weight, while searches for saffron supplements highlight a consumer desire for naturally-derived supplements.

Supplement brand JShealth is growing in popularity indicating an increased consumer interest in optimising hair health from the inside out. The growth in searches for Lemme is driven by a variety of Kourtney Kardashian's products: Chill, Focus, Sleep and Matcha. The consistent growth in searches for Cymbiotika is a good example of the impact of branding as top search queries are for the brand itself as opposed to a specific supplement. An increased interest in Truvani is largely driven by its protein powder, and Golo for their diet pill.

Ingredient-wise leptin is popular as consumers look for new ways to support weight loss, and L-citrulline to potentially support strength-based exercise. Saffron searches in supplements highlight consumer interest in naturally-derived ingestible ingredients. Growing interest in 5-HTP and Inositol indicate an interest in supplements that could be beneficial for both physical and mental wellbeing.

Top searches such as glycolic acid body lotion, breast milk soap and vanilla lotion suggest consumers’ increasing desire for ingredient-driven products. The growth in searches for cleansing oil and shimmer oil highlight an interest in oil formulations when it comes to bodycare.

The growth in popularity of brands such as EOS and Native highlight the importance of accessibility in bodycare products like lotions and body wash. Maison Francis Kurdjian has also seen a boost, driven by the Baccarat rouge 540 body oil, demonstrating how a brand can use its signature focus, such as an iconic scent, to break into different product categories. An increase in searches for Goodwipes point to consumers’ interest in cleansing products that are both environmentally friendly and portable.

Current top ingredient searches include vanilla, sesame and honeysuckle, revealing a growing interest in fragrance when it comes to bodycare products. The growth in searches for glycolic acid suggests that consumers are increasingly eager to look to skincare ingredients traditionally used on the face for the body as well.

Top growing trends like pistachio perfume and honey perfume reveal that consumers are interested in sweet, natural scents. Interest in pheromone perfumes reveal consumers are looking for products that do more than just smell good, with scents that some believe to evoke feelings and physiological responses.

Increased searches for top brands, such as Ex Nihilo and Tamburins, indicate that consumers are open to experimentation and looking beyond accessible labels. Trending brands like Dedcool and Sol de Janeiro underscore the impact of distinctive scents with less traditional product formats, such as mists, creams and even laundry detergent.

Top growing scents such as pistachio, ginger and blueberry reveal consumer interest in fresh scents this season. Growing searches for amber indicate the popularity of warm scents as well.

The top growing nail trends indicate that consumers are interested in textures and finishes this season — including chrome powder, aura nails and velvet nails. Meanwhile, searches for BIAB (“builder in a bottle”) nails and rubber base gel reveals consumers are looking for new formulations when it comes to nail products.

Searches for Pear Nova and Glamnetic reveal that consumers are interested in press-on nails. Growing interest in Nine Ze Lacquer, ILNP and Rogue Lacquer suggests a trend for bright, fun colours with interesting finishes.

The top-searched benefits reveal that consumers are paying more attention to the product formulations of nail products. The searches also highlight consumers’ preference for durability and ongoing interest to find the best product for them.

Top searched makeup trends like face liquid bronzer and face bronzer stick indicate consumers are searching for products to give them a bronzed look for summer. An increased search interest in clear blush indicates consumers are paying more attention to innovative, unsuspecting formulas. Searches for both pot concealer and matte concealer shows a consumer desire for products that come in a variety formats.

Top growing face makeup brands such as Sheglam, Merit, and Rare Beauty are being searched for a variety of colour complexion products including blushes and contour sticks. Searches for Dr Hauschka highlights a consumer desire for products with a purpose beyond aesthetics — particularly with natural or medicinal ingredients. Searches for Kaja indicate interest in blush and water-based primers with a K-beauty influence.

The top growing benefits like glowing and brightening reveal the types of looks consumers are prioritising this summer season. Searches for water- and oil-based makeup trends reveal that consumers are becoming more educated, and therefore are seeking out specific product formulations when it comes to face products. The search for hydrating makeup supports the trend of consumers looking for skincare-like claims in makeup products.

Top skincare searches such as snail serum and snail facial show consumers’ willingness to set aside concerns of slimy texture for the sake of hydration. Skin patches are growing in popularity, with face patch and star pimple patches currently top searches for consumers looking to tackle skin concerns. Interest in nanoneedling indicates that consumers are looking at non-invasive procedures to achieve desired results.

Continued interest in Florence by Mills shows the staying power of some celebrity brands. The growth in searches for Futurewise may come off the back of its alignment with a popular trend: slugging. Searches for Michael Todd Beauty and Pharmaciopy indicate interest in skincare tools and brands accessible through Amazon.

Growing searches relating to skincare for birch juice, cica and snail mucin indicates consumers are seeking naturally derived ingredients that support healing and hydration. Searches for polypeptides and copper peptides highlight consumer interest in skin-supporting proteins.

Saffron and lion's mane highlight a desire for consumers to get supplemental benefits from naturally derived ingredients. Searches for BC30 probiotics indicate how consumers are becoming more educated around probiotics and are seeking out specific types. Searches for HMB supplements reveal consumers’ desires for muscle growth, whereas inositol supplements searches are related to an increased interest in weight loss help.

Top searches for the likes of Cymbiotika and Arrae show consumer interest for the brands themselves, as opposed to a variety of products, revealing the impact that strong branding can have on supplements. Searches for Truvani indicate consumers’ desire for protein supplements that support their muscles, while interest in Nutrafol demonstrates how consumers are looking for ways to support hair health from the inside out.

Searches for Ingredients like saffron, lion’s mane mushroom and castor oil highlight an increased interest in naturally derived supplements to aid their concerns. Searches for HMB and BC30 probiotics suggest that consumers are looking beyond the standard probiotic or muscle support supplements, as they gain a wider education of the benefits of specific ingredients and forms.

Top trends such as body shimmer oil and glitter lotion reveal that consumers are strongly interested in a bodycare product that makes skin sparkle and hydrates. Searches for antibacterial bar soap, whitening soap and breast milk soap reveal that consumers are looking for hygiene products to treat specific concerns or skin conditions.

Labels such as Versed highlight consumer interest in products that take skincare ingredients below the neck. Searches for Maison Francis Kurkdjian also show a growing desire for body care that is driven by consumers’ favourite scents. Consumers searching for Native are looking for “natural” and accessible products, while those searching for Head & Shoulders are open to using their shampoo as a body wash.

Searches for vanilla and sesame oils reveal consumers’ desire for fragrant and hydrating bodycare ingredients, respectively. Searches for hyaluronic acid and retinol in bodycare products indicate consumers are looking to bring skincare ingredients to larger-format products. The interest in breast milk may be due to consumers’ desires to use natural products to solve concerns.

Searches for pheromone and skin perfumes reveal that consumers are looking for fragrances that have an effortless, animalistic effect. Meanwhile, searches for mini perfumes highlight the ongoing desire for consumers to have fragrances suitable for travel and an affordable way to try new fragrances before purchasing a full-size.

Trending brands such as Sol de Janeiro and Dedcool have gained traction with scents that cross product formats. Searches for brands such as Nishane and Ex Nihilo reveal that the modern consumer is interested in more premium niche scents as well.

Trending scents such as bourbon and vanilla reveal a consumer trend for gourmand fragrances, with good-enough-to-eat notes. The search for gooseberry and blueberry highlight the rising search for fresh, fruity smells.

The top trends reveal a strong interest in chrome nail aesthetics. Whether green chrome, chrome french or blue chrome, consumers are looking for a variety of ways to achieve metallic, ultra-shiny nails. Searches for polygel suggest a desire for innovative nail products.

Consumers are looking for accessible options in nail care, and modern nail designs with non-toxic formulas and easy-to-use applications are top of searches.

The top-growing colours and finishes highlight a desire for radiant, eye-catching summer nails. Chocolate nails reference the “chocolate glazed donut nails” trend coined by Hailey Bieber’s nail artist Zola Ganzorigt. Searches for chrome, iridescent and shimmery finishes supports modern nail enthusiasts’ desire for nails that shine.

Top makeup trends, such as goth eyebrows, passport makeup and chav makeup are highly visual looks that first gained popularity on TikTok, demonstrating the social platform’s influence in driving global aesthetics. The search for two tone lips offers an opportunity for brands to explore new lip styles, while searches for bleached eyebrows alongside skin tones and hair types reveal that consumers are looking for visual examples of this trend across different demographics.

The top search queries driving makeup indicate an interest in complexion products such as foundation and blush, reminding brands to highlight complexion products for the summer. The growth in searches for Florence by Mills and Rare Beauty reveals ongoing interest in celebrity-led lines. Kiko Milano is gaining traction within US search, demonstrating new opportunities for the Italian brand among American consumers.

The top growing makeup benefits reveal that consumers are looking for products that leave them with a bright and healthy look. Searches for water-based items also indicate that consumers are becoming savvy with product formulations, revealing a preference for different formula nuances – something for brands to consider when it comes to product positioning.

There is a growing trend among consumers to embrace more immediate solutions for skin concerns, seen in the form of nanoneedling, lasers and facials. Consumers are also showing preference for multi-balms due to their functionality and ease of use. The rising interest in snail serum, along with the snail facial, indicates that consumers are willing to overlook foreign textures and potentially uncomfortable sensations in exchange for results, such as intense hydration.

Across these top-growing skincare brands, consumers are looking for reviews. Searches for these brands are driven more by the brand name than by a specific product, highlighting the significance of branding and visibility for today's consumer.

The top growing skincare ingredients reveal that hydration and anti-aging concerns are top of mind for consumers. Many of these high-growth ingredients are being driven by branded searches, highlighting the importance of brands creating products that prominently feature key ingredients.

There is a growing trend among consumers to seek out haircuts that are considered more masculine and involve shorter lengths that are closer to the scalp. Consumers are using hair gems to express their unique style and are also using hair tools, such as volumising irons, to add flair to their hairstyles. Additionally, there is growing interest in pre-washing hair, indicating a willingness among consumers to rethink traditional routines.

Consumers are showing interest in wigs, demonstrated by the enduring popularity of premium human-hair brands such as Hairvivi and Recool Hair. Concerns related to hair loss are also prominent, particularly when searching for Hims, which offers both prescription and nonprescription hair loss treatments. There is also growing demand for products that address root cover-up and grey hair, as seen in brand searches for Arey and Color Wow.

Searches encompass a variety of forms but oils are emerging as a prominent format. Notably, there has been a growing fascination with holistic and botanical formulas and ingredients, as indicated by the increased interest in ayurveda in search trends. Many of the popular ingredients are searched for their ability to support hair growth and density.

Sustained riser: Steady growth over the past years, these trends are safe bets.

Seasonal riser: Seasonal trends that are likely to come back even stronger.

“Very low / No competition” indicates there are little to no brand searches alongside a trend.

“Low competition” indicates that there are a few brand searches alongside a trend.

“Medium competition” indicates that there are some brand searches alongside a trend.

“High competition” indicates that there are several brand searches alongside a trend.

“Very high competition” indicates there are many brand searches.

#6997. A Brutally Honest Editor’s Guide to Amazon’s Black Friday iPad Deals

The iPad Mini and iPad Air are $100 off, but I’m forecasting steeper steals.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

As a shopping editor who tracks prices on Apple products all year, I have high standards. Truth be told, Apple tech deals have had some highs and lows this year: some items reached their lowest prices ever during major sale moments like Prime Day, while others (I’m looking at you, Labor Day deals!) have been less than impressive. Now that Amazon’s 12-day Black Friday sale is here, I’m creating an official guide to the iPad deals you should shop now...and which are worth waiting a little longer for.

I’m forecasting steeper deals during the day of Black Friday (November 27), but that doesn’t mean you’re doomed to wait. Ahead, you’ll find an updated guide to all the iPad models on sale right now:

So far, the best Black Friday iPad deal up for grabs is $100 off the iPad Mini. This small but mighty tablet is powered by the speedy A17 chip, with a 12MP camera that can capture 4K videos. It’s compact at 7.7 inches tall and weighs less than a pound (0.66 pounds, to be exact), which makes it the perfect size to toss in your purse for on-the-go streaming and note-taking.

Though this is the steepest iPad deal thus far, it still pales in comparison to last year’s discount. This exact model was a record-low $349 during last year’s Black Friday sale, so there’s a good chance it’ll get even cheaper in the days to come.

You can also score $100 off the latest iPad Air model. It’s powered by the M4 chip, which boasts advanced graphics and a powerful processing system that multitasks with ease—whether you’re editing videos, jotting down notes, or creating presentation slides. When paired with the Magic Keyboard, it can function more like a laptop than a typical tablet. It’s available in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes, with storage ranging from 512GB to 1TB.

Price-wise, this isn’t the best discount I’ve ever seen. It’s been on sale for as low as $519, a whopping $130 cheaper than its current sale price. Even though it’s the steepest deal available right now, there’s a strong chance that it drops in price on Black Friday.

Another iPad deal I’m keeping an eye on? The 11th-generation iPad, which was released in 2025. Although its current $50 discount isn’t particularly impressive, I saw it drop below $300 during last year’s Black Friday sale. I recommend holding out just a little longer to get a better deal.

Compared to the iPad Air, this model sacrifices some processing power for a more affordable price point. The A16 chip is better suited for tasks like scrolling your TikTok feed, flipping through your e-book library, and streaming the Love Is Blind finale, so it’s a great option if you prefer using your iPad in recreational settings. It comes in three storage sizes—128, 256, and 512GB—with the best discount on the 128GB model.

All in all, the iPad deals available right now aren’t worth writing home about—but don’t despair! These deals can literally change in an instant, and I’m predicting that prices will become comparable to last year’s Black Friday sale if you’re willing to wait until next week. Ahead, I’ve rounded up a few more iPad models worth keeping tabs on.

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Looking to score one for yourself? We rounded up top-notch options from Dunhill, Percival, and more.

You don’t necessarily need a car coat. If you’re in the market for a new coat and not, like us, learned in the world of 20th century menswear, it just might be one of the few styles you’ve heard the word for—peacoat and trench coat likely being two others. All three are great if you’re looking for something a bit grown up than your average off-duty jacket. A trench coat would give you gravitas, a peacoat versatility; the car coat, though, strikes a nice middle ground. Find the right one, and it can replace 90 percent of your other coats.

At its inception, the car coat was a heavy outer layer. Cars were still open to the elements, so the rich who owned them needed floor-length fur jackets to keep themselves warm as they went motoring and did a lap around the neighborhood on Christmas. As cars became more more enclosed and more part of daily life, the car coat became more practical. The length got shorter—eventually settling around mid-thigh—to be comfortable when you sit in the driver seat but with enough coverage to be considered a coat. Materials shifted away from furs to leather and suede, then to even lighter-weight gabardines and weather-resistant materials. They

But current iterations of the car coat don’t exactly follow a formula. As we’ve seen with Harringtons, brands just start to use the most widely-known phrasing to get guys into buying a coat. We, in the interest of keeping some amount of historical accuracy, will stick to a formula. A car coat has that mid-thigh length, a turn down collar, and a practicality for someone getting in and out of a seat. They’re great during fall, and they can be worn through winter if you live somewhere that doesn’t get consistently below freezing. Here, you’ll find our favorite picks.

We’re starting on the high end, but it’s only because if you’re looking for a by-the-book garment or accessory tied to motoring history, you go to Dunhill. In its original form, Alfred Dunhill’s company sold motoring accessories. Overcoats, goggles, picnic sets, horns, lamps, dashboard clocks—the tagline was “Everything but the motor.” It was a luxury men’s brand for the premier luxury hobby of the time.

The company has gone through several iterations, but has always maintained a bend towards that luxury man. Now, under the creative direction of Simon Holloway, it’s a standard-bearer for a slightly more fashion-forward vision British menswear. Take this car coat for example. It calls back to the house’s original business model, and it is classic in its finishes: turn down collar, natural shoulders, cuff straps, and totally un-adorned through the torso. But the fabric is a gorgeous wool, silk, and cashmere blend. It’s a genius balance between tradition and fashion, one that only Dunhill is well-positioned to put out.

Length: mid-thigh Material: 84% wool, 13% silk, 3% cashmere

Now that we’ve gotten the formalities out of the way, let’s talk value. For the money, Percival is the best on this list. Hell, it is really just the best on this list overall.

The fabric is the same you’d find on a trench—a tight-weave polyester and cotton blend. The cut is simple and easy to wear. The length, crucially, is more suited to the modern driving experience. There’s a bit of bum coverage, but if you were out running errands and getting in and out of the car, you can keep the coat on. We also love the classic colors and patterns the team cut this in.

All of that for an attainable price, it’s one of the best items in the Percival lineup.

Length: just over your rearMaterial: 65% polyester, 35% cotton

Short of finding an Etsy seller, this is probably the closest you’ll get to the genuine car coats of the ‘50 and ‘60s. The fabric flutters just around your knees just like they did way back when, while a classic collar and navy blue hue adds to the retro nostalgia. Made of 100% cotton, the fabric is finished with C0 water repellency and lined with cotton to give the fashion even more function. We’d recommend wearing and styling like you would a trench (though, if you want something more substantial, J.Crew also makes the Rivington in cozy wool for those who in search of a new winter coat.)

Length: mid-thigh, grazes the kneeMaterial: 100% cotton

If you liked all the above, but didn’t totally love the over $500 price tag—check out H&M. Similar silhouette and weight. Different material and color.

Length: just a little below the kneeMaterial: Polyester 94%, Rayon 5%, Spandex 1%

This one doesn’t need much explaining. Imagine the iconic Burberry trench, cut to a more modest car coat shape.

This bridges a little more into topcoat territory, but its mid-thigh length balances it back into a car coat classification. Still, if you live in a more temperate climate and are in the market for a more substantial cold weather layer, look no further.

Length: Mid-thighMaterial: 50% Wool, 45% Recycled Polyester, 5% other

Lean into the polished look of a car coat by opting for a herringbone pattern. It’ll bring an extra layer of coziness (both literally and figuratively) to the overall look.

#6992. Quilted Liner Jackets Are the Swerve Your Wardrobe Needs. Here Are 10 Stellar Picks.

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Layering is the name of the game in fall and winter. For the next few months, you are not a person; you’re a living, breathing Russian nesting doll. You are encased in strategic layers of t-shirts, sweaters, scarves, light jackets, and big jackets that you divest yourself of over the course of a day (or night). Like a knight donning his armor, you will spend this season dutifully putting on and taking off each of these individual pieces as you fight the seemingly endless battle against winter.

A few pieces are a given. A good tee certainly isn’t going anywhere, nor is a sweater. The specific kind of Big Coat you use varies depending on the guy and his style, but it’s nevertheless a guaranteed winter staple. Those middle layers can be a bit of a toss up, though, which is how you might encounter something like a quilted liner jacket.

Once upon a time, these padded jackets served as the interior protective shell worn under World War II era flight jackets before expanding into more mainstream outerwear. The quilted padding traps body heat, but doesn’t make the jacket so heavy that it just feels like another cumbersome layer. You can still wear it as a liner jacket—but lowkey, if it’s the right temperature, they also work pretty well on their own. So if you’re in the market for a new versatile transitional weather jacket, you’ve come to the right place.

If we had to pick one from this entire group, it would be this jacket from Buck Mason ... And it’s really not that close. Inspired by old-school mountaineering outfits, the nylon is woven in Japan, and the down fill has an exceptional warmth rating. Add a elastic cuffs and a fit that works layered underneath or overtop, it’s perfect.

Look, layering’s great and all—but no one talks about how annoying and awkward it is when you get hot enough to take off one layer, but then are stuck just kind of holding onto it until you get the chance to put it down or hang it up. That’s not a problem with this packable Paul Smith shirt jacket. Let it do its magic to keep you warm. When you’re ready to take it off, simply collapse it down, zip it up, and stuff it away into your pocket until you need it again.

Rains has a well-established reputation of balancing fashion and function with their outerwear, whether it’s their Esquire-editor favorite Fishtail Parka or this bomber liner jacket. Nothing beats a classic leather bomber...except maybe the rain (leather + rain = no bueno). That’s not an issue with Rains’ Banja bomber liner. You get that same edgy look, but with a slightly more practical construction. Plus there’s something sleekly minimal about the channel quilting. Layer it beneath your actual bomber or heavy coat of choice for optimal warmth all season long.

Look, we love a good Dickies moment. They make some of our favorite pants of all time, not least of which because they’re mad affordable—though that’s a pretty big element to it. So naturally, if someone comes up to us asking for a high-quality and stylish quilted liner jacket at well under $100, we’ve got one word for ya: Dickies.

Barbour’s been making sturdy outerwear that can withstand the rainy U.K. weather since the 1800s. And while they don’t strictly make a liner jacket, this lightweight—or “Flyweight,” as Barbour calls it—quilted jacket gets pretty close.

With a sleek, collarless design, this Fieldworth jacket can easily slide under any heavy coat. It falls more into “middleweight jacket” territory, meaning it’ll probably keep you toastier than some of the other options on this list—both on its own and when layered up.

If you’re looking for more of a typical fall/spring jacket, J.Crew’s PrimaLoft® jacket is where it’s at. The quintessentially Americana brand uses the down alternative to create a well-insulated transitional weather jacket you can layer with, or wear on its own.

Look, all these other brands and designers are great and all—but Alpha Industries is the real deal. No like seriously. When the company was first founded in Tennessee in the 1950s, it was as a clothing contractor for the United States Department of Defense. These were the guys making those sexy flight jackets long before Tom Cruise shrugged one on in Top Gun. Their Deco Liner nods to the OG liners of yore, featuring a slim, collarless design that will integrate with additional layers. Wear the jacket by itself when you start feeling warmer, and let the whole world see the Alpha embroidery on the back so everyone knows this is some top of line shit.

If you’re in the market for something lighter and less padded, opt for this cotton hunting jacket. The silhouette takes inspiration from vintage Czech military liners and traditional hunting gear to create a layer of outerwear breezy but still warm.

Get two jackets for the price of one with this reversible number from Cos. You get all the benefits of a quilted coat, with the versatile sleekness of a classic collarless jacket.

#6991. The Rise of the Maximum Visibility Bra

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The summer of 2014, I was a college student working at a small-town lingerie store that lined its walls exclusively with neutrals. Every day, I sold women flesh-toned bras—black if they were really feeling kinky—all while filling my own intimates drawer with the same styles. Undressing in front of a guy that same summer, he voiced genuine disbelief over my nude, industrial-strength strapless bra. He wasn’t so much confused over its gravity-defying function as the fact that it was there, at all.

The early 2010s set a nearly impossible goal for young women: naturally perky breasts without any apparent scaffolding. But that’s all changing. Pop princess Adela’s exposed bras have become as central to her identity as her electric pink hair. Once left to jiggle freely beneath semisheer cotton, Charli XCX’s chest is now more often displayed in intricate lingerie. Several months back, Saint Laurent’s Spring 2027 front row was littered with boudoir-inspired looks while Prada and Fendi literally sent bras-as-tops down the runway. Bras have come out of hiding.

Somewhere between the “free the nipple” movement in 2012 and the impending #MeToo revolution of 2017, boobs became less of a sexualized spectacle and more of a political battleground. Victoria’s Secret canceled its fashion show as basics-driven intimates brands like Cuup and Arq gained traction for destigmatizing natural shapes. Then, breasts bounced back into cultural focus. The shift might be credited to the climate—conservatism generally propels women to take shelter in traditional femininity, or it is thrust upon them—as well as the twin forces of Sydney Sweeney and semaglutide weight loss. Either way, women got thinner while their chests grew larger—reflecting a beauty standard we hadn’t seen in a generation. Implants entered a new era of demand and dialogue, as celebrities like Kylie Jenner and Megan Fox transparently joined the big-breasted brigade.

But boobs aren’t just bigger—they’re bolder. Gone are the days of basics and bralettes. It’s all about va-va-voom underwire, satin, and lace—even push-ups have returned to the conversation. Still, “there’s a difference between showing your bra and showing off your bra,” discerns Tara Ocello, director of brand marketing at intimates brand Skarlett Blue.

Last month, the recently revived Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show broadcast Jenner strutting down the runway, her 445-cc-moderate-profile silicones outfitted in a record-breaking $50 million bra. Bella Hadid, Candice Swanepoel, and Adriana Lima showed off the iconic mall brand’s finest embroidered balconettes, lacy push-ups, and satin plunge bras. Angels aside, the reintroduction of these runway collections is also indicative of a shift in consumer product demand—a spokesperson for Victoria’s Secret claims there’s “strong interest” in fashion-forward details like lace, satin, logo hardware, and the brand’s statement shine straps. The Very Sexy Push-Up Bra remains the number one of the three mainline bras in its “Very Sexy” category. “Today’s customer wants a bra that performs beautifully and deserves to be seen,” says a Victoria’s Secret spokesperson. “It’s expanded how customers engage with [our bras] as both foundation pieces and intentional styling elements.”

The luxury London retailer Agent Provocateur has been positioning its designs as statement pieces since it launched in the mid-’90s—the last time exposed bras enjoyed prevalence. Creative director Sarah Shotton noticed the trend bubbling several years back on the Glastonbury grounds and immediately returned to the design studio. “We predicted this and designed [for it] about a year and a half in advance. I am constantly thinking, could it be worn as an outerwear bra?” she says. “I think if customers are going to invest in it, they want it to work harder than just in the bedroom. Lingerie as outerwear is just getting bigger and bigger.”

Category transcension is, of course, good for business. Victoria’s Secret reported sales up 10 percent in its second quarter, and Agent Provocateur has also seen revenue growth this year. Eager to capitalize on the movement, contemporary brands like Lioness are now engineering built-in underwear to imitate the effect of an exposed bra. This week, Charlize Theron wore a similar style by Tom Ford to the Governors Awards.

I have, undoubtedly, been influenced. This year, I have spent more money at Victoria’s Secret than cumulatively on lingerie in the past decade—acquiring my own Very Sexy Push-Up, and a turquoise polka-dot number. These are bras I’ve never gravitated toward, let alone purchased, because they seemed like impractical additions to my wardrobe. I’ve had to ask myself: Can you wear leopard-print under a white tee? What if the lace breaches my neckline?

Somewhere between Erin Brockovich and Blake Lively’s character in The Town, an exposed bra—particularly a colorful one—became a media shorthand for unsophistication, and more often than not, sexual availability. In simpler terms: tacky. Now, tacky is trending. Along with diamanté-encrusted snapbacks and sky-high peep-toes, straps in dynamic hues are stretched across the décolleté of It girls en masse. Printed cups are peeking out of the necklines. Some fashionistas are forgoing the shirt altogether. “There's a real cultural shift from polished perfection toward something more expressive, unpredictable, and a little undone,” claims Ocello. Or, perhaps a little more human.

This certainly isn’t a trend for everyone. According to Shotton, Agent Provocateur’s biggest sellers are corsets—a style that was once also considered strictly lingerie, but has since sashayed into the light. One wonders if their popularity is a gateway to full bra-baring, especially as GLP drugs become more readily available, and women more comfortable in their bodies. But with a Blue Wave washing in Woke 3.0, how long do boobs—and their bold accessories—have left? In all seriousness, might we look back on this moment with the same disdain we once reflected on early-aughts raunch culture? Only social media will tell. In the meantime, I plan for my collection to keep growing.

#6986. Who Is Daddy Franklin From ‘The Body’? For Starters, Nnamdi Asomugha Is Kerry Washington’s Husband

Daddy Franklin is married to Olivia Pope?

If you watched The Body in one sitting and are now fully obsessed with it, you’re not alone!! The horrifying coming-of-age series is scary good, and while you may not be familiar with the actor who plays Father Samuel Franklin (aka Daddy Franklin), you definitely know his very famous wife. As it turns out, Nnamdi Asomugha has been married to Kerry Washington for over 13 years now, having fallen in love after watching Kerry perform in Race on Broadway in 2010. Kerry later confirmed the story during a 2018 interview with Marie Claire, saying, “The last time I did theater, it completely transformed my life. That’s where I met my husband.” Cute!!!

Though things got off to a rocky start (Kerry apparently told Nnamdi she didn’t date athletes, and Nnamdi told Kerry he didn’t date actors), the two got together anyway, and just about three years later in June 2013, they tied the knot in a super low-key ceremony. According to their marriage license, Kerry and Nnamdi said “I do” in Hailey, Idaho, where Nnamdi’s sister officiated and Kerry’s parents served as witnesses. Since then, the couple has welcomed two kids together—Isabelle Amarachi, born in 2014, and Caleb Kelechi, born in 2016—and are seemingly thriving outside of the spotlight. But we think it’s time to learn a lil bit more about Nnamdi, don’t you?

Here’s everything you should know about the man behind Daddy Franklin, including how he rose to fame as a former NFL cornerback and what he’s up to next.

After growing up in Louisiana in a Nigerian Igbo household, Nnamdi attended the University of California, Berkeley, where he played for the California Golden Bears football team. Soon after graduating, Nnamdi was drafted in the first round of the 2003 NFL Draft by the Oakland Raiders, which is very impressive.

Over his 11-year professional football career, Nnamdi also played for the Philadelphia Eagles and the San Francisco 49ers, and in December 2013, the cornerback signed a one-day contract with Oakland so he could retire as a Raider. I love to see a loyal man!

According to Nnamdi, the decision to retire at 32 was difficult, but it still felt like the right time for him. “Yeah, I felt that it was a good time, but it didn’t make it any easier,” he told UPROXX. “It’s a game that 'til this day I miss, and I miss playing. It’s not that I want to go play again, but I miss so many aspects of it; being around the team, being around the coaching, that calm before the storm.”

Nnamdi first caught the acting bug all the way back in 2008, when he landed the role of “Party Guest with Wife” on the CW sitcom The Game. (Remember: There are no small roles, only small actors!!) He then caught the eye of director Peter Berg on the set of a Nike commercial shoot in 2009, who was impressed by the athlete’s ease in front of the camera. From there, Nnamdi went on to play small roles in Friday Night Lights, Leverage, and Cubed before making his on-screen feature film debut in 2012’s Fire with Fire.

Since retiring from the NFL, Nnamdi has fully committed himself to his acting career with starring roles in the films Crown Heights, Sylvie’s Love, The Good Nurse, The Knife, and—most recently—The Body. He’s also served as a producer on several of those projects as well.

Despite all his success, Nnamdi still remains as modest as ever, avoiding social media and press to instead focus on his craft. “I’m really bad at self-promotion. I know that about myself,” he previously explained to Bleacher Report back in 2017. “People told me all of the time, ‘You could be such a big star if you just talked about yourself more,’ but I’m not good at that. It’s always been about team.”

During a 2018 interview with Today, Kerry corrected a host when they alluded to her two children, saying, “I’m a mother of three." The reason: Nnamdi has a now-teenage daughter from another relationship, who Kerry has helped raise alongside her two biological children. And just like with Isabelle and Caleb, the couple keeps their eldest far from the paparazzi, so very little is known about her.

As Kerry joked to People, “I have moments where I take pictures or videos of one of my three amazing kids and I wanna post it online, and I tend to just send it to my parents or my shrink instead.”

Philanthropy is important to Nnamdi, which is why he created the Asomugha Foundation in 2005 at the very beginning of his career.

The foundation has two main programs: Orphans and Widows in Need (which provides food, shelter, medicine, vocational training, literacy efforts, and scholarships to widows and orphans in Nigeria) and Asomugha College Tour for Scholars (which takes selected students from Bay Area and Los Angeles area high schools on college tours across the country).

Though Kerry and Nnamdi are both actors and producers, it isn’t often that they work together on creative projects. Back in 2017, Nnamdi told Vanity Fair that it was possible he and his wife would co-produce a project at some point.

“We would produce,” he said. “We’d probably produce before acting, I would think.” The following year, his production company, iAm21 Entertainment, helped produce American Son, a Broadway play starring Kerry, and hopefully, that won’t be the last time the two are involved in the same project.

As far as sharing the screen goes, however, Nnamdi doesn’t think that will ever happen. As he told The New York Times, “I produced American Son, but as actors, there’s no plan as of now for that collaboration. We’re very supportive of each other’s journeys, but we’ve always been that way. We always want the best for each other in whatever we’re doing.”

Case in point? The couple’s *chef’s kiss* appearance at the 2025 Met Gala. Ahem:

Oh, and the duo’s 2025 Golden Globes looks:

And ofc, he was right by Kerry's side during her December 2024 Hollywood Walk of Fame ceremony, where she finally received her well-deserved star. How cute do they look with Kerry's parents??

TL;DR: Kerry and Nnamdi truly couldn’t be any cuter. Keep on being adorably low-key, you two.

#6984. Why Men Are Posting Thirst Traps in Red Light Face Masks

Gonzalo Fernández Escribano knew all about the benefits of red-light therapy for his skin. Fewer wrinkles, a brighter complexion, minimizing acne—he’d experienced it all firsthand when he tried out LED masks during his facials. In March 2025, he purchased one for at-home use. Little did he know it would come with an extra benefit as a provocative prop for a sexy photo.

"I use my red-light mask right before bed, so I’m already shirtless,” says Escribano. “Let’s just say the sexy-looking picture is easily convenient to take.”

Escribano is one of many men online who’ve embraced the red-light thirst trap. More and more, image-conscious guys with followings built around some combination of beauty, fitness, wellness, travel, are pairing their red-light routines with the occasional shirtless selfie. The trend is especially prevalent in gay-male internet culture, where faceless torsos shots, sometimes featuring beefy chests and six-pack abs, have been part of the visual language of dating apps and social media for years. A shirtless red-light-mask pic is a variation on the theme: The body and the anonymity are still there—only now there’s a skincare routine attached.

Jayson Stacy, a celebrity groomer, noticed his friend wearing an LED in his Instagram profile picture three years ago. At the same time, Stacy had recently gotten a mask himself and decided to follow suit, posting a photo of his own after Mardi Gras under the guise of some much needed recovery.

“It’s almost like a sexy Halloween costume, but you don’t have to wait until October,” Stacy says. Escribano agrees, saying it makes him look like a superhero. Strong shadows, glowing skin, and a Sith-like red glow mix together in a thirsty trifecta meant to slow someone’s scrolling.

For Stacy, red-light masks strike the perfect balance between wellness and plausible deniability. “You’re supposed to use the mask after you wash your face, so most are fresh out of the shower before using,” he says. “It’s like, ‘Oh, look at my morning routine,’ which gives the perfect excuse to be mostly unclothed. Then you have the mask on, you feel like someone can’t see your face, so it can feel like a layer of protection.” In other words, the skin care routine becomes the reason for the thirst trap, even though it’s only half the motivation.

Red-light therapy is a noninvasive treatment that uses low-level LED light to stimulate cellular activity and boost collagen production. The technology has become especially prominent over the last few years thanks to its ability to reduce inflammation, soften fine lines, and promote skin and muscle recovery and hair growth. (That is, as long as you are willing to invest in high-quality equipment and use it every single day).

Celebrities have been documenting their LED routines for years, from January Jones to Kim Kardashian. But those posts were mostly framed around the masks’ intended purpose: improving your skin. Somewhere along the way, though, a certain breed of extremely online men—trainers, models, artists, content creators, and guys who simply know their angles—found a second purpose for the masks: as an accessory for a hot photo. The masks are turning up in bathroom mirror pics, bedroom shots, and buried several slides deep in otherwise unrelated photo dumps, often without any mention of skin care at all. And judging by the comments—fire emojis, heart eyes, and the occasional “yummy”—their followers seem to be noticing something other than the mask.

The thirst traps are also surfacing on social media at a time when curiosity around red-light therapy is booming. A 2025 study analyzing Google Trends data found that search interest across red-light-therapy-related terms increased 118% after February 2024. And by 2025, Google reported that searches for “red light therapy” had reached an all-time high. As these futuristic devices have rapidly flooded our feeds, maybe it was only a matter of time before they made their way out of the skin care selfie and into something a little thirstier.

In some ways these images are being ushered into well-trodden territory. In 2021, TikTok’s viral Silhouette Challenge had users transform themselves into barely distinguishable, body-forward silhouettes under a red filter, turning the color itself into a visual shorthand for sex appeal. Meanwhile, for gay men, shirtless photos are hardly a novelty, especially on dating apps like Grindr and Sniffies, where headless torsos are practically part of the experience. “The headless torsos definitely all blend together at this point,” says John Arthur Hill, who compares swiping through hookup apps to looking into “a lukewarm batch of Chili’s skillet queso” and trying to figure out what’s cheese, meat, or a bell pepper.

And even when the most impressive six-pack can get lost in an endless doom scroll, red light can add just enough intrigue to get someone to look twice. For Adam Pent, an OnlyFans creator who’s no stranger to posting thirst traps himself, that curiosity is part of the appeal. “It [a red-light-mask thirst trap] is definitely more interesting because I’d be curious about who’s behind the mask,” he says. To Pent, there’s something creative about the whole thing. “I guess it makes the photo a bit more artful too? ‘Art thot’ vibes I guess, unless it looks like sponsored content.” It also makes him want to shop. “I’m less focused on the body and more like, ‘Should I just get one already?’”

The red-light thirst trap also holds a certain mysterious appeal. “I’ve been posting ‘masked’ selfies for quite some time because I think it’s a really hot aesthetic and such a cool fantasy,” Michael Anthony, a celebrity makeup artist, says. For him, it’s not just about looking good in the photos. “The fantasy of anonymity and pleasure, while doing something for yourself that will make you look and feel better—it’s all so sexy.”

An LED face mask is a luxurious way to get an at-home glow, and Shark's is one of our favorites. It helps to fight acne and fine lines, and it can help depuff around the eyes for those long nights.

Tattoo artist Alvin Archibald sees a similar appeal. “There’s a subtle tension between vulnerability and control that makes it interesting,” he says. “The mask takes away your facial expressions, so the body becomes the focus. It creates this interesting dynamic where you’re both exposed and concealed at the same time. There’s something almost intimate about it, like you’re getting ready for an audience without necessarily admitting it.”

#6983. We Really Need to Talk About the MobLand Season 2 Finale

A certain character’s fate hangs in the balance.

Nothing is simple in MobLand. Two seasons in, the plot has racked up more lines than Eddie put up his nose the night he stabbed Tommy Stevenson in season 1. Actually, that’s not strictly true. One thing is simple in MobLand: Eddie. He is a simpleton of truly Homeric (as in Simpson) proportions: a smarmy, sneering, simpering Freudian mess, channelled with gimlet-eyed precision by Anson Boon. All he wants is his God-given right to be respected.

Trouble is, when you’re an anti-Midas who turns everything he touches to shit, respect is a dish that never leaves the kitchen. Eddie is, in Kevin’s words in season 1, “a knifey little twerp.” That stabbing set the whole bloody saga in motion, so it’s only right that two seasons later we end with Eddie the Incompetent. Full circle, then, like a roundabout made of corpses.

MobLand opened with Eddie turning a stabbing into a gang war, so it seems fitting that we end with Eddie turning an assassination into an own goal. But we’ll get to that.

It seems Conrad’s chickens are coming home to roost, and his marbles are jangling around his head like loose change. We open the episode with his card being declined at a petrol station. In frustration, he shoots the till boy dead. But he knows what it means.

“We’re getting lifted,” he tells Maeve in the car. Police are raiding the entire business: bank accounts are frozen, warrants are out, and Tattersall is telling reporters the Harrigans have links to terror groups across the globe. The family convenes at a dingy old safe house out of town.

“We’re terrorists,” says Seraphina. “We’re looking at life in Guantánamo. It’s now or never.”

Her plan has been bubbling for a while. She calls it Harrigan 2.0: going global.

Remember the diplomatic suitcase of diamonds Seraphina collected from her billionaire stepdad Charlton in the last episode? It was meant to fund her and Bella’s takeover of the Harrigan operation. Now, it seems, Harry has it. He takes her aside to let her know he knows. “How did you know?” she asks, incredulous.

Then he says the three words he says more than any others in MobLand: “It’s my job.”

Inside the safe house, the family are all there, and everyone has a plan to pitch. Kevin wants to crawl back to Kat and hand over Conrad, Maeve, and Eddie. “Clean the house,” he growls to Harry, out of earshot of the others.

Conrad, meanwhile, isn’t sure what to do. “What are our options?” he asks Harry.

“We don’t have any,” comes the terse reply. “Either we run seven ways and it’s every man and woman for themselves, or we go back to Kat and try to strike some kind of deal.”

Kevin proposes offering her 50 percent and first working out who’s a liability. “And right now I’m seeing a lot of liabilities. Right, Harry?”

Bella has had it up to ’ere with Kevin’s pusillanimity. “Oh, you nearly got to the end of a sentence without saying ‘Harry,’” she taunts. “I know he saved you from a bumming once but… Jesus.”

Kevin pulls a pistol and fires, missing her ear by millimeters. Conrad draws. “Put the gun down, boy,” he hisses. Bella steps forward. “Go on then, big boy.”

You could cut the tension with piano wire.

“Fuck this, I’m getting us out of this mess,” says Seraphina, defusing the standoff by fetching a fistful of diamonds from the car. “Fifteen Type IIa brilliants. North of ten million euros,” she tells Conrad, placing them in his hand.

The plan: offer Kat a cut of the empire. “This time tomorrow we’re back in business.”

Remember that glorious, long-winded speech Conrad gave in Spain about the good old days, how he came from nothing, and how Maeve has been his compass through the carnage of his life? “We were born outlaws and we’ll die outlaws,” he bellowed.

Well, now he knows the jig is up. Looking balefully at the floor, he grunts: “Do it.”

So how will Harry play this? He slips out to his 4x4 and rings Kat. “At 5 p.m. I will meet your diplomatic courier. I will pass to said courier €10 million in untraceable diamonds. Upon authentication, I will give you the location of the Harrigan family.”

A double cross? It must be a ruse. He simply MUST have a plan… Then, hanging up, he mutters: “Fuck this, I’m done.”

He returns to the family and lies: “Kat will take the ten million and 50 percent.” Too easy by half.

As Frankie put it two episodes ago: “Is that it? Unless you’ve got some brilliant plans, that is actually a bit shit. What are you up to, Harry?”

We’re more than halfway through and haven’t heard a peep from Frankie, our laconic, crocodilian villain. Ah, but here he is, getting the news of Harry’s volte-face from Tattersall. “How do we know it’s not a bluff?”

“He’s not stupid,” says Tattersall. “He knows when the game’s up.”

“Well, you know me,” leers Frankie. “I can’t resist a gamble.” Guns are grabbed from car boots, and off he pootles with a gaggle of tooled-up goons to send the Harrigans back to Hell.

It’s all unfolding very quickly now, as denouements always should. Back at the safe house, Conrad is still seeing the dead, including the petrol station lad he just murdered. Maeve says he’s been saying their names in his sleep.

The old loon’s marbles are now departing his head like passengers from a cancelled flight. But there’s one thing that’ll straighten any man out: a black pearl of Maeve wisdom. “We’ve been stuck up tighter holes than Kat McAllister’s,” she reassures him. “But when you’re stuck up someone’s hole, there’s at least two ways out.”

Quite so. And who better to lead the way than Harry? As ever, he picks the exit that leads straight back to where he came in. Unbeknownst to us, he has gone up Kat’s backside, rummaged about, and come out the other end holding her entire career. The “betrayal” was a ruse from the start.

So when Frankie’s goons arrive armed to the teeth, it’s a trap: flash grenades, smoke grenades, poison gas, and Zosia on the exit with a machine gun for anyone daft enough to run. “Oh, Harry,” concedes Frankie, before a mighty gunfight erupts and Harry tears through the house like Keyser Söze in a gas mask. “So this isn’t the beginning of a beautiful friendship,” smiles Frankie, choking in the corner. Harry shoots him in the knee.

Then Harry rings Kat. Those “untraceable” diamonds? Very traceable indeed, straight to a terrorist organization. He has bribed a low-ranking diplomatic courier to deliver them along with a “little present, just for you.”

She opens the box, ashen-faced. It’s Donnie’s blue and rotting head. “This one you might find harder to justify,” he tells her.

“My family are gonna hunt you down and feed you your balls,” she spits.

“Probably,” says Harry. “But not before they feed you yours.”

Checkmate, Kat. The black queen has no more squares to go.

But wait … Harry can offer her one square. “I can fix this,” he says.

Here’s what she’s going to do. She’ll resign. She’ll kill the police investigation. The Harrigans’ accounts will reopen and they’ll come off the terror list.

Cut to a London corridor of power, where a faceless civil servant informs DS Kavanagh that “continuation of your terrorism financing line will interfere with an active joint intelligence operation between British and American security services. You will stand down at the close of business.”

And so, full circle. Maeve is electrocuting Frankie’s balls with a car battery. Kevin is building bridges with Bella. Conrad is going madder by the day. And Eddie?

The Semtex he blackmailed Paul for was meant for Harry, at Maeve’s behest. In the hands of any other Harrigan, this would be a doddle. But not Eddie. Not the knifey little twerp, a man who could trip over his own foreskin in an empty car park.

And he does. But first, the hints. Something strange has been going on with Jan all episode: the soppy Damien Rice soundtrack, the wistful dream sequences of the good times she shared with Harry. Her Harry. The one she fell for in the first place. She seems to have forgiven him. They’re even taking a family holiday.

But there’s one last stop before they go: Harrigan HQ, where Eddie is lying in wait. While Harry negotiates the terms of the holiday with Conrad, Gina and Jan stroll over to the lake. It’s Eddie’s moment, his chance to shine. He plants the Semtex in their car, hides around the corner, arms the bomb, finger hovering over the detonator … then a phone call.

By Finn McCool’s cobblers, it’s Kelly “Mad Dog” O’Connor, the lunatic son of the Medusa, whom Maeve sent Eddie to kill. “I’m coming for you,” growls the voice. “The Mad Dog is coming.”

Gina, Jan and Harry return to the car. Only Jan gets in. In his quivering, fearful state, Eddie trips and drops the detonator.

That’s Jan up in smoke, along with Harry’s plans for a quiet life. It may spell the end of Jan and all her problems, but it’s only the beginning of Eddie’s. He now has Mad Dog O’Connor to answer to, and Harry.

Then the credits roll, and what a gloriously cruel place to leave it.

The only other loose end is Frankie. We’re left to assume he met a long, painful death at the business end of Maeve’s car battery, but we never see a body. I truly hope he does a Harry and wriggles out of one last tight hole—Maeve’s hole—with one good knee and a long memory.

Season 3 can’t come soon enough. When Harry works out whose finger was on the detonator, Eddie’ll wish a knifey little twerp is all he could be.
